name: Veeraraghava Perumal Temple, Thiruvallur
deity: Vishnu as Veeraraghava Perumal, reclining on Adishesha, with the Goddess Kanakavalli Thayar
period: A Divya Desam of Thondai Nadu, sung by Thirumangai Alvar and Thirumazhisai Alvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham
summary: At Thiruvallur, the Thiruevvul of the hymns, Vishnu reclines as Veeraraghava Perumal beside the healing Hrithapapanasini tank — a Thondai Nadu Divya Desam sung by Thirumangai and Thirumazhisai Alvars.

sections.history: Thiruvallur, known to the hymns as Thiruevvul, is a market town west of Chennai whose life has long turned around its great Vishnu temple. Here the lord reclines as Veeraraghava Perumal, the valiant Raghava, with the Goddess Kanakavalli Thayar in her own shrine. It is one of the 108 Divya Desams, the abodes of Vishnu sung by the Alvar saints in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, and belongs to Thondai Nadu, the northern Tamil country. Thirumangai Alvar and Thirumazhisai Alvar sang of the lord here, and the acharya Vedanta Desika later praised him too. The temple is attributed to the Pallavas of the late eighth century, and the Nayaks of Thanjavur are among those who enlarged it in later centuries.
sections.architecture: A seven-tiered rajagopuram rises over the entrance, and a granite wall encloses the courts within. In the sanctum the lord lies on the coils of Adishesha in the serpent-couch posture, a long and majestic image that fills the shrine; above it rises the Vijayakoti Vimana. Pillared halls lead inward, with a separate shrine for Kanakavalli Thayar. Beside the temple lies its tank, the Hrithapapanasini — the remover of the heart's afflictions — whose waters are central to the life of the shrine.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells of the sage Salihotra, who bathed in the tank and kept a long penance of fasting. When at last he prepared his meal, an aged Brahmin came to his door asking for food, and the sage gave it gladly. The guest then asked, "Evvul?" — "where may I lie down?" — and the sage offered his own hermitage. The visitor lay down and revealed himself as Vishnu, and from that question the place took its old name, Thiruevvul.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps two Brahmotsavams, in the Tamil months of Chithirai and Thai, when the processional deity is carried through the streets of Thiruvallur. Vaikunta Ekadashi draws great crowds, and new-moon (Amavasai) days are especially observed: devotees come in large numbers to bathe in the Hrithapapanasini tank and worship the reclining lord.
sections.experience: Thiruvallur is an easy journey from Chennai, and many come on new-moon days to bathe in the tank before darshan, trusting in its old reputation for easing troubles of body and mind. Inside, the long reclining form of Veeraraghava Perumal is the heart of the visit; pause, too, at the shrine of Kanakavalli Thayar.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions and a midday closure; new-moon days, Vaikunta Ekadashi and the Brahmotsavams are busiest. Confirm current timings before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruvallur lies about 45 km west of Chennai on the suburban rail line towards Arakkonam, with frequent trains from Chennai Central; the temple is a short ride from Thiruvallur station. The nearest airport is Chennai.
